title: Red McKenzie's prejudice
summary: Bunn says Red McKenzie was prejudiced although he used the Spirits for his sessions, as is true of St. Louis generally.

story.theme_name: Race and segregation in the jazz life
story.community_name: Segregation on the road and the bandstand

blocks.x: That's a nice one.
Yeah, it works pretty good. You know, it's -- for home, home recording quality, it's pretty nice.
Uh-huh.

There was a couple of things we didn't get on the tape yesterday, you know, we shut it off and then we were talking some more and some things came out. One of the things was we were talking about Red McKenzie.
Red McKenzie.
Yeah. And you said that he was prejudiced.
He was.
Difficult to work with for that reason.
Yeah. That attitude.
Uh-huh. How did this come out? I mean, how did he --
Well, we done our sessions, you know, and got it over with, and that was it.
No. I mean, how did -- he wasn't too prejudiced to use the Spirits.
No.
To back him up.
No, no. But I mean his attitude, you know.
Of course, you know, he was white and so forth, and we was colored and so forth, you know. And his attitude was a lot different then. A lot of people (Unintelligible).
So it was like maybe dealing with other white people, you'd come up with some stuff?
Yeah. He lived in St. Louis.
Did he know the Daniels brothers from St. Louis, do you think?
Uh-uh. They all met back east, with the Spirits.
Did you run into that a lot with white musicians, or just a few in those days?
Well, Red was -- he was all right with us.
Uh-huh.
As far as that's concerned, you know. But we could tell, you know, about him being prejudiced, he was, from that town he was from. St. Louis, you know.
Yeah.
That's a very prejudiced town, because I worked there too, with the Spirits.
